power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape.

Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains.
Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty.
Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain.
We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles.
First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding.
Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings.

Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data.
We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches.

In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.
In our everyday lives, visual beauty can be found all around us, in artworks and landscapes, and in objects and scenes.
One can experience beauty unexpectedly while cycling to work or deliberately in a museum.
In both cases, encountering beauty enriches our lives and brings us joy.
How can we explain visual beauty, and which factors determine a stimulus's aesthetic appeal?
These questions have been asked since Fechner's first empirical investigations on image preferences in the nineteenth century (Fechner, 1876; Bader, 2018).
text.formatted: These questions have been asked since Fechner's first empirical investigations on image preferences in the nineteenth century <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Fechner, 1876;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bader, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We have come a long way from these classical studies.

Based on decades of empirical research, we now have different theoretical models that characterize the biological basis of visual aesthetics (Leder, 2004; Palmer et al., 2013; Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014; Redies, 2015).
text.formatted: Based on decades of empirical research, we now have different theoretical models that characterize the biological basis of visual aesthetics <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Leder, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Palmer et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Redies, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although these models differ in proposed mechanisms and stress different cognitive processes, they all converge on the notion that sensory processing is the critical backbone: Models assume "perception" (Leder, 2004), "sensory-motor" (Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014), or "sensory coding" (Redies, 2015) steps, where sensory features are the first stepping stone towards aesthetic appeal.
text.formatted: Although these models differ in proposed mechanisms and stress different cognitive processes, they all converge on the notion that sensory processing is the critical backbone: Models assume "perception" <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Leder, 2004)</ref>, "sensory-motor" <ref type="bibr">(Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014)</ref>, or "sensory coding" <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Redies, 2015)</ref> steps, where sensory features are the first stepping stone towards aesthetic appeal.

text.text: The importance of visual features in aesthetic appreciation is well established.

Studies in empirical aesthetics have identified a range of low-and mid-level visual features associated with aesthetic appeal, including curvature (Corradi et al., 2019; Vartanian et al., 2024), color (Graham et al., 2016; Schloss & Palmer, 2011; Swartz et al., 2024), complexity (Van Geert & Wagemans, 2020), and symmetry (Rhodes et al., 1998; Huang et al., 2018), among others.
text.formatted: Studies in empirical aesthetics have identified a range of low-and mid-level visual features associated with aesthetic appeal, including curvature <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Corradi et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Vartanian et al., 2024)</ref>, color <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Graham et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Schloss & Palmer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Swartz et al., 2024)</ref>, complexity <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Van Geert & Wagemans, 2020)</ref>, and symmetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Rhodes et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huang et al., 2018)</ref>, among others.

text.text: Visual features can reliably explain domain-specific beauty (e.g., symmetric vs asymmetric faces) and unveil shared aesthetic preferences (e.g., preferences for curved rather than angular objects).

More recently, studies have shown that combining multiple features into predictive models can yield powerful predictions of aesthetic judgements for static (Iigaya et al., 2021) and dynamic (Ekinci et al., 2026) stimuli.
text.formatted: More recently, studies have shown that combining multiple features into predictive models can yield powerful predictions of aesthetic judgements for static <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Iigaya et al., 2021)</ref> and dynamic <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ekinci et al., 2026)</ref> stimuli.

text.text: This shows that multiple visual features are reliably and systematically linked to perceived beauty.
Yet, even though we have learned a lot from these studies, answers to a more general question remain elusive: Why are these specific features preferred?
For instance, why is a curved object preferred over a rectilinear one?
Why is a symmetric face preferred over an asymmetric one?

Though for each of these examples, individual explanations have been proposed (Rhodes, 2006; Bar & Neta, 2006), we argue that there may be overarching computational principles, which are fundamentally ingrained in human visual processing, and which may explain perceived beauty across individual features and across stimulus domains.
text.formatted: Though for each of these examples, individual explanations have been proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Rhodes, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bar & Neta, 2006)</ref>, we argue that there may be overarching computational principles, which are fundamentally ingrained in human visual processing, and which may explain perceived beauty across individual features and across stimulus domains.

text.text: In other words, they may ultimately at the same time explain why we prefer curved objects and symmetric faces.
In the following, we use computational principles to refer to neural coding motifs in sensory systems.
Such neural coding motifs form specific and recurring patterns of neural information processing that characterize or constrain the processing of visual information in the brain.
Critically, we ask whether and how we can identify computational principles that are indicative of perceived beauty -without necessarily being tied to individual features or stimulus domains.
A useful starting point for thinking about such computational principles is to ask why the visual system should represent the beauty of visual inputs in the first place.
A tractable proposal is offered by processing fluency theories (Reber et al., 2004; Graf & Landwehr, 2015), which posit that beauty arises from enhanced processing efficiency in sensory systems.
text.formatted: A tractable proposal is offered by processing fluency theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Reber et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Graf & Landwehr, 2015)</ref>, which posit that beauty arises from enhanced processing efficiency in sensory systems.

text.text: This idea offers concrete suggestions for candidate computational principles: Neural motifs that facilitate efficient coding in resource-limited sensory systems should be linked to perceived beauty.

Computational principles consistent with such efficient coding may include neural motifs that reduce neural competition through integration (Röth et al., 2021), increase efficiency by sharpening representations (Pouget et al., 2000), integrate sensory inputs with predictions based on prior expectations (Rao & Ballard, 1999), or facilitate neural communication through oscillatory dynamics (Fries, 2015; Stecher et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Computational principles consistent with such efficient coding may include neural motifs that reduce neural competition through integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Röth et al., 2021)</ref>, increase efficiency by sharpening representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pouget et al., 2000)</ref>, integrate sensory inputs with predictions based on prior expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Rao & Ballard, 1999)</ref>, or facilitate neural communication through oscillatory dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fries, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Stecher et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While these candidate principles are an arbitrary subset, they can all operate across multiple levels of the visual hierarchy and thus transcend individual feature or stimulus preferences.

As these examples also illustrate, there are numerous candidate principles that facilitate efficient representation in the visual brain, and there are potentially several different neural indicators for each of them.
Establishing reliable links between a computational principle and perceived beauty therefore requires tedious, time-consuming, and expensive experimentation.

As an alternative, however, modern artificial neural networks (ANNs) offer cheap and high-throughput in silico testbeds, where computational principles can be examined at scale and in turn linked to human beauty ratings (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: As an alternative, however, modern artificial neural networks (ANNs) offer cheap and high-throughput in silico testbeds, where computational principles can be examined at scale and in turn linked to human beauty ratings (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: Once a candidate principle has been identified, it can be computationally benchmarked in an ANN architecture using a set of suitable measures.
Variations in these measures can then be linked to variations in beauty ratings across stimuli.
After establishing links between a computational principle in an ANN and perceived beauty in human observers, this association can be biologically validated using targeted human neuroimaging.

This validation is important, given that ANNs, although in many cases suitable for modelling human vision (Kietzmann et al., 2017; Cichy & Kaiser, 2019; Doerig et al., 2023), can show systematic divergences from human perception and neural processing (Xu & Vaziri-Pashkam, 2021; Bowers et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This validation is important, given that ANNs, although in many cases suitable for modelling human vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kietzmann et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cichy & Kaiser, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Doerig et al., 2023)</ref>, can show systematic divergences from human perception and neural processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Xu & Vaziri-Pashkam, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bowers et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the following, we show the feasibility of this framework by highlighting two recent studies that used ANNs, and specifically deep neural networks (DNNs), in conjunction with brain imaging data to identify, benchmark, and validate computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty.

Specifically, Tang et al. text.text: These findings suggest that lower energy expenditure in the human visual system, similarly to lower processing costs in visual DNNs, is indicative of greater perceived beauty.
As in the DNN, this association was strongest for complex feature representations in category-selective regions of highlevel visual cortex.

To sum up, this study first hypothesized metabolic cost to be a candidate principle tied to visual beauty, then used DNN benchmarking as a testbed for this association and in turn validated the association using human neuroimaging data.
The resulting association between metabolic cost and perceived beauty not only shows the feasibility of the proposed framework.

It also highlights a computational principle (energy efficiency) that can operate across multiple stages of the visual hierarchy and thus promises exploratory power beyond individual features and stimulus domains.
Further support for this principle comes from a related study that investigated the sparsity of DNN representations for faces and paintings (Dibot et al., 2023).

text.text: Starting from fluency-based considerations, too, Nara and Kaiser (2024) investigated a complementary computational principle that increases coding efficiency: integrative processing.

Inspired by human neuroimaging work (MacMains & Kastern, 2011; Kaiser et al. 2014; Kaiser & Peelen, 2018), they hypothesized that the efficient integration of image elements across space would reduce processing demands via a compression of information into holistic representational formats.

text.text: The consequently lower processing demands should lend greater beauty to images that are more readily integrated across space.
The authors thus hypothesized a positive correlation between the degree of spatial integration and perceived beauty across images.
The hypothesized association was again benchmarked in a computational model and then validated using human brain data.
Computational benchmarking.
For computational benchmarking, the authors used a VGG16 model pre-trained on scene recognition (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014; Zhou et al., 2017).

text.text: The degree of spatial integration for each image was measured as the signinverted correlation of DNN activity patterns for the whole image and an average of the activity patterns for complementary image halves (generated from opposing checkerboard patterns overlaid on the image).

Lower correlations were taken as indicative of more integration (i.e., the whole is differently represented from the halves), whereas higher correlations were indicative of less integration (i.e., the whole is similarly represented to the halves).

Across images, the degree of integration in the DNN, and particularly in intermediate to late layers, was positively correlated with beauty ratings from an independent group of human observers (Fig. 1D), confirming the hypothesis that perceived beauty is linked to how efficiently the brain integrates information across whole images.

text.text: This relationship remained robust across four experiments with different sets of natural images, from landscapes to varied real-world scenes.

To validate the relationship between integrative processing and beauty using biological brain data, the authors conducted an fMRI experiment where observers passively viewed a subset of natural scene images and image halves.

Akin to the DNN analysis, correlations of fMRI response patterns across the whole scene and the two complementary halves were used to quantify integrative processing, with lower whole-to-halves correlations indicating more integration and greater whole-tohalves correlations indicating less integration.

Confirming the computational benchmarking, integrative processing was positively correlated with perceived beauty across the visual cortex, with a significant correlation obtained in scene-selective PPA (Fig. 1E).

Integrative processing provides another great example of a computational principle that can operate across feature hierarchies and across stimulus domains.

Both highlighted studies follow a very similar framework to test and validate candidate neuro-computational principles, combining modern artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for benchmarking and neuroscientific experiments for validation.
Their approach exemplifies a new line of research with a hypothesis-driven neurocomputational framework (Fig. 1A).
text.formatted: Their approach exemplifies a new line of research with a hypothesis-driven neurocomputational framework (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: They also highlight the feasibility of this framework for establishing overarching principles in the neural coding of beauty, which transcend the feature preferences identified in previous work.
Now, how can we further build on this framework?
There are already other candidate principles on the horizon that could be benchmarked and validated using the proposed framework.
Spatiotemporal redundancy seems promising in this regard.
We know that, already at the photoreceptor level, neuronal signals are reformatted into a decorrelated representational format to decrease redundancy and increase efficiency (Dan et al., 1996).
text.formatted: We know that, already at the photoreceptor level, neuronal signals are reformatted into a decorrelated representational format to decrease redundancy and increase efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dan et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Similar processes operating across the whole visual hierarchy can make use of the predictability of information across space and time.
This redundancy reduction could be related to perceived beauty, as decreasing redundancy will yield more fluent processing of the compressed inputs.
While this constitutes just one promising example of a candidate principle, many others are readily testable using the framework we highlight here.

These could include principles such as representational sharpening (Pouget et al., 2000), prediction-error minimization (Van de Cruys & Wagemans, 2011), and an optimal balance between feedforward and feedback communication (Herz et al., 2020), each constituting a distinct computational mechanism underlying aesthetic processing.
text.formatted: These could include principles such as representational sharpening <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Pouget et al., 2000)</ref>, prediction-error minimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Van de Cruys & Wagemans, 2011)</ref>, and an optimal balance between feedforward and feedback communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Herz et al., 2020)</ref>, each constituting a distinct computational mechanism underlying aesthetic processing.

text.text: While many of these principles are directly derived from fluency-based theories, other theoretical views may posit different candidate principles.
For instance, reward-based models of aesthetic value also emphasize that current and expected future learning predict aesthetic experiences (Brielmann & Dayan, 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, reward-based models of aesthetic value also emphasize that current and expected future learning predict aesthetic experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brielmann & Dayan, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Other candidates could be derived from pioneer theories of aesthetics, such as Berlyne's psychobiological theory (1971), in which complexity and novelty are related to beauty in a U-shaped curve, and Martindale's cognitive theory (1988), which suggests prototypicality and meaningfulness are determinants of beauty, yielding a fresh look at classically proposed mechanisms.

text.text: When using ANNs in service of distilling computational principles that are biologically derived and interpretable, we can find new explanations for why certain stimuli are preferred over others.
This approach is complementary to using ANNs as prediction machines in the context of maximizing accuracy in predicting whether or not a stimulus is preferred.
ANNs, like DNNs, naturally excel at this task, with their high-dimensional representations offering powerful predictions of human beauty judgments when directly regressed onto them.
For instance, Conwell et al. (2025) showed that a set of 180 different ANN architectures trained on visual recognition could robustly predict human beauty ratings.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Conwell et al. (2025)</ref> showed that a set of 180 different ANN architectures trained on visual recognition could robustly predict human beauty ratings.

text.text: By now, similar findings have been obtained across a range of studies and domains (Lu et al., 2014; Seresinhe et al., 2017; Jin et al., 2019; Nara & Kaiser, 2024).
text.formatted: By now, similar findings have been obtained across a range of studies and domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lu et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Seresinhe et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Jin et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Nara & Kaiser, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, such studies largely rely on "brute-force" approaches, where many features are jointly exploited to enable high-accuracy predictions.
Unlike the approach proposed here (Fig. 1A), this essentially leaves the underlying mechanisms hidden in a black box.
text.formatted: Unlike the approach proposed here (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>), this essentially leaves the underlying mechanisms hidden in a black box.

text.text: This does not necessarily mean that such approaches cannot yield insights further down the line, where opening the black box and examining the high-dimensional representations that drive predictions can yield further insights.

For instance, a recent study by Soydaner and Wagemans (2026) predicted aesthetic evaluations using human-rated image attributes by employing different machine learning models trained on those attributes.
text.formatted: For instance, a recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Soydaner and Wagemans (2026)</ref> predicted aesthetic evaluations using human-rated image attributes by employing different machine learning models trained on those attributes.

text.text: To clarify the importance of each feature, they used an explainable AI technique, Shapley Additive Explanations, by measuring how the prediction performance changes when excluding and including each feature across different combinations of other features.

This technique allowed them to assess the contribution of specific features to predicting aesthetic evaluations while exploring whether there is a nonlinear relationship between aesthetic evaluations and network features.
In the future, further research along these lines may unify approaches based on first principles and approaches based on maximizing predictive power.

Finally, using ANNs to benchmark candidate computational principles also highlights a critical feature of ANNs in cognitive neuroscience: The approach leverages ANNs as scientific tools for exploring hypothesis spaces (Cichy & Kaiser, 2019; Wichmann & Geirhos, 2023).
text.formatted: Finally, using ANNs to benchmark candidate computational principles also highlights a critical feature of ANNs in cognitive neuroscience: The approach leverages ANNs as scientific tools for exploring hypothesis spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cichy & Kaiser, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Wichmann & Geirhos, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Here, the power of ANNs as reasonably good models of human visual processing enables cheap and high-throughput testing of hypothesized associations, which in turn can be validated in bespoke human experiments that use targeted paradigms and stimuli.

In the future, this computational exploration of putative effects can even be fully automatized into an iterative hypothesis generation and testing loop (Lu et al., 2024; Musslick et al., 2025; Kabra et al., 2026) that automatically produces a set of computational principles that can then be validated.

text.text: At this point, it is important to stress that we do not advocate for an approach that replaces studies on feature preferences.
Such studies are critically important for characterizing the building blocks of visual preferences within and across domains.

We rather advocate for a complementary approach that coexists with studies of feature preferences, providing a new starting point for adding explanations for feature preferences on a more abstract level of description.
But how do we go forward and bring these approaches together to distill such explanations?

After identifying neuro-computational principles (e.g., metabolic cost or integrative processing), we can use these new insights and directly test whether established feature preferences can be derived from these first principles.

Taking the example of metabolic cost, the common reason curved lines are preferred over angular ones, and symmetric faces are preferred over non-symmetric ones may be that they are both coded more fluently, requiring less energy expenditure in neural circuits.

Following this example, one could utilize previous stimuli in experiments relating curvature and beauty (or symmetry and beauty), compute the desired measure in an ANN (here: metabolic cost), and test whether it is systematically related to curvature and whether the shared variance in turn explains human beauty ratings.
Work along these lines thus has the potential to unite approaches based on computational principles and studies focusing on feature preferences.
Some first steps in this direction have been made.

For instance, Nara and Kaiser (2024), in their spatial integration study, tested which visual features contributed most to spatial integration in DNNs and found that the integration of high spatial frequency contours was most prominently linked to the prediction of perceived beauty.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Nara and Kaiser (2024)</ref>, in their spatial integration study, tested which visual features contributed most to spatial integration in DNNs and found that the integration of high spatial frequency contours was most prominently linked to the prediction of perceived beauty.

text.text: This was achieved by manipulating the visual feature content of the images while repeating the in silico benchmarking in their DNN models.

Moving forward, however, it may turn out to be relatively tricky to relate individual visual features and a stimulus optimally "fulfilling" the computational principles in question: Most everyday stimuli are defined by a myriad of visual features and relevant dimensions, and a stimulus may reach an optimal point in this feature space through intricate interactions between its many features.
Identifying overarching computational principles also promises to reconcile the literature on feature preferences in cases where it does not fully converge.
A good example is the relationship between complexity and perceived beauty.

While some studies found that complexity relates to beauty following an inverted U-shape (Berlyne, 1971; Nadal et al., 2010), others reported negative or positive linear relationships (Tinio & Leder, 2009; Nadal et al., 2010; Delplangue et al., 2019).

text.text: If we can identify computational principles that explain why complexity is related to beauty, we can then scrutinize under which conditions certain stimuli and domains produce different types of relationships between complexity and beauty: The different relationships observed in different studies may directly follow from a differential alignment with the more overarching coding motif that relates complexity and beauty in the first place.
Here, our focus has been strictly on perceptual processing and how it relates to beauty.
However, it is possible that the framework proposed here offers a fruitful starting point for investigating the cognitive processing related to beauty, too.
For one, computations in cognitive systems may also systematically link to perceived beauty.
For instance, fluency is not constrained to sensory systems.

The fluency of processing at different levels of information processing can also predict cognitive judgments (Oppenheimer, 2008), such as judging fluent statements to have higher truth (Reber & Schwarz, 1999) or believing fluent-named companies in the stock market to have better values (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2006).

text.text: From an aesthetic perspective, Brielmann and Dayan (2022) suggested that decision-making plays a critical role in our aesthetic preferences, and applying fluency considerations to decision-making processes could be a promising avenue for characterizing computational principles on a cognitive level.

text.text: Additionally, cognitive systems may read out sensory beauty by evaluating perceptual representations in line with their overarching properties, such as how compressed and sparse they are.
It has been shown that higher-level neural correlates of beauty operate on re-weighted sensory representations (Iigaya et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It has been shown that higher-level neural correlates of beauty operate on re-weighted sensory representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Iigaya et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It is conceivable that cognitive systems do not read out visual feature codes directly when assessing beauty in the world.

They may rather read out the quality of a representation and whether coding is in line with principles that are shared across sensory inputs that have been associated with beauty in the past (Walther, 2026).
text.formatted: They may rather read out the quality of a representation and whether coding is in line with principles that are shared across sensory inputs that have been associated with beauty in the past <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Walther, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Understanding what these principles are would consequently open new ways of thinking about the nature of such high-level representations.
In conclusion, the framework proposed here offers a new methodology for understanding the nature of visual preferences.

First, the framework focuses on establishing broader principles of aesthetic processing rather than limiting the scope of the explanations to single perceptual features using a single type of content.

Second, through recent advancements in ANN modelling, it offers new opportunities to overcome critical challenges in empirical aesthetic research by (i) enabling a fast testbed for computational hypotheses and (ii) distilling computational principles that can be compared with those observed in the human brain.

We believe that this approach has the potential to kickstart a fruitful new line of investigations into the neural correlates of beauty, which may ultimately yield explanations for why we assign beauty to the world around us.
